# The Liberal Balance of Power and the Four Horsemen of Its Apocalypse 

Jack Snyder

Jack Snyder 

Jack Snyder is the Robert and Renée Belfer Professor of International Relations in the Department of Political Science and the Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies at Columbia University. His books include Human Rights for Pragmatists: Social Power in Modern Times.

## Abstract

Jack Snyder argues that liberalism’s historical success rests on four competitive mechanisms: free markets, democratic elections, an open marketplace of ideas, and a distinctively liberal approach to the balance of power. These mechanisms’ effectiveness depends on a “visible hand” of laws, norms, expertise, institutions, and social practices that regulates competition and guards against instability. For the fiftieth anniversary of International Security, Snyder applies this framework to the contemporary crisis of the liberal order and the rise of illiberal nationalism that stems in part from deregulation, economic inequality, political polarization, media fragmentation, and attacks on democratic guardrails. He argues that the post-1945 liberal order worked better than previous illiberal and laissez-faire liberal alternatives because market competition was embedded within welfare states, Bretton Woods institutions, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and democratic accountability. In international politics, liberal powers have outperformed authoritarian challengers because liberal institutions enable more effective strategies, alliance cooperation, learning, and self-correction. By contrast, authoritarian “late developers” often respond to economic and security vulnerabilities through self-destructive strategies of militarized autarky and imperial overexpansion. Snyder nevertheless acknowledges liberal overreach, especially in peripheral “forever wars.” He recommends renewing democratic alliances, reforming the defense industrial base, steering clear of peripheral military interventions, rebuilding a constructive media environment, and developing socially embedded liberal institutions capable of addressing contemporary economic and technological problems.

The United States and the liberal international order have had their ups and downs over the half century since the inception of this journal. In volume 2 (1977), the founder of American realism, Hans Morgenthau, pronounced the United States already in “decline” as a result of the Vietnam War. 1 In volume 15 (1990/91) of International Security, Stephen Van Evera proclaimed that liberalism’s triumph in the Cold War had left Europe “primed for peace,” but John Mearsheimer warned that the coming anarchy would take Europe “back to the future” of the 1930s. 2 Now, at the journal’s fiftieth anniversary, the United States and other established democracies are assaulted by illiberal domestic trends at the same time as they are challenged by the rising assertiveness of authoritarian great powers. President Donald Trump’s tariff wars, disdain for U.S. democratic allies, chumminess with illiberal strongmen, and hostility to the rule of law at home and abroad have led many to conclude that the liberal international order is already dead. 3 

Despite these unprecedented twists and turns in world politics, military alignments around Eurasia nonetheless still conform loosely to a pattern that has been familiar for at least two centuries. The more liberal, system-organizing great powers and their allies have formed an encircling, balancing alliance to contain the unruly behavior of late-developing, authoritarian great powers that have profited from their niches in the liberal global economy but nevertheless chafe under the demands of rules that are poorly matched to their political systems.

Authors writing in International Security have provided many of the concepts and the empirical context that are needed to make sense of the challenges to the liberal order. They have been at the forefront of debates on realist power politics and liberalism, including authors who see these perspectives as complementary. 4 Some International Security authors have performed autopsies on the “rules-based international order” to assess whether it was ever truly liberal and functional. 5 Others have pointed out that the United States still produces 26 percent of global economic output, the same as during the “unipolar moment” in the 1990s, and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s liberal democracies still command over half of the world’s economic and military power. International Security articles debate whether China’s growth and power have already peaked or are still climbing, and whether the United States still has the capacity and will to lead a balancing coalition to contain Chinese and Russian aggression along the Eurasian perimeter. 6 

This uncertain juncture calls for a probing diagnosis of liberalism’s strengths and weaknesses to know what to keep, what to jettison, and what to reform. 7 Liberals have been accustomed to viewing their social order as a set of mutually reinforcing rules and practices in which all good things go together: high per capita income, a thriving civil society with free speech and free media, rule of law with due process protecting personal and economic rights, impersonal public administration, and accountable democratic government. As if guided by Adam Smith’s invisible hand, all this once seemed to mesh in a way that produced unequaled prosperity, superior political stability, and powerful international alliances uniting liberal states in a peace among free-trading democracies. 8 After World War II, these liberal powers built on their victories to codify effective rules for an unprecedently open, stable, and productive liberal order covering much of the globe, but now all this seems in doubt. 9 What went wrong, and can the liberal system be fixed?

I argue that four seemingly automatic invisible hand mechanisms have indeed been at the core of liberalism’s success as a social order: free market competition aligning individual interest with social efficiency and welfare, free competition for votes empowering the prudent median voter, the free marketplace of ideas exposing public discourse to effective scrutiny and constructive debate, and a liberal approach to the balance of power, which has enabled the more liberal major powers to prevail in six out of the last six struggles for international hegemony, from the Seven Years’ War through the Cold War. 10 When used well, these four mechanisms of liberal social equilibrium have solved problems of economic uncertainty and political complexity, efficiently coordinating action by aligning individual incentives with collective benefits through decentralized means.

Critics of the liberal order, however, have argued that the U.S.-led system was not nearly as open, consensual, and rules-based as its proponents have proclaimed. Rather, they say it has been exploitative, opportunistic, hypocritical, prone to instability, and riddled with fundamental contradictions that are now reaching crisis proportions. 11 These incongruities include the tensions between free markets and political equality, frictions between a global economy and national self-determination in politics, and the contradiction between the core liberal assumption of individual self-interest and the original meaning of “liberality” as generosity toward others. 12 The concept of the invisible hand is crucial for understanding how to reconcile these contradictions.

Liberals’ claims for the automaticity of these liberal equilibria are part mythic metaphor, part self-serving ideology, and part aspirational holy grail. 13 Liberalism’s worst moments at home and abroad have come when the invisible hand has failed to reconcile individual interest with social welfare in a stable political order. At particularly dire junctures, such as the Great Depression of the 1930s and now, liberalism’s four horsemen have not spontaneously pulled together, led by a benignly ordering invisible hand. For all four mechanisms, the success of purportedly self-regulating systems has depended on strengthening the visible hand of norms, laws, social practices, expertise, and institutions that embed these self-adjusting mechanisms in an effective regulatory system that harnesses and moderates the “creative destruction” of the free market. 14 

Effective regulation in all these realms works not by overruling the results of decentralized competition but by enabling the conditions under which competition can be efficient and stabilizing. Liberal systems need both entrepreneurial incentives that reward efficient competitors who provide “abundance” and a welfare state that ensures social stability through broad distribution of benefits. 15 Supply and demand in liberalism’s markets for goods, votes, and ideas can incentivize efficiency and stability when foundational rules set up a competitive system, while manually operated corrections fine-tune its results. 16 Liberal systems can deviate from beneficial outcomes when regulation is absent or when it is misguided or predatory. Sometimes manual adjustments are needed to ensure that these markets operate competitively, as in anti-monopoly action by state regulators, legislators, and the courts. Conversely, sometimes manual adjustments are needed to dampen rampant competition, such as agreeing to limit arms racing when offensive military technologies are perceived to have an advantage. 17 Under realistic assumptions, liberal mechanisms of competition do not spontaneously settle into stable, efficient equilibria, but they come far closer to doing so than illiberal systems—close enough to work well when publicly accountable experts oversee making the right adjustments. 18 

The liberal balance of power works in much the same way. As John Ruggie notes, “balancing behavior” is a widespread mechanism in international anarchy, even though perfectly effective balances of power do not automatically form to prevent armed aggression. 19 Robert Jervis argues similarly in his work on system effects that the balancing of power is an inherent tendency in international anarchy, but achieving stabilizing results from strategies of deterrence, containment, and spheres of influence depends on knowledgeable, constructive adjustments in a zone of discretionary choice. 20 

Although liberal powers have far outperformed illiberal powers in managing this balancing game in the past, more recently liberalism’s domestic and international systems of the invisible hand have often seemed self-defeating rather than self-correcting. 21 A major reason is that liberalism’s regulatory structures have been under assault or used counterproductively in recent decades. 22 As a result, there is a gap between liberalism’s laissez faire mythology and its actual management of its four systems. As they did in the 1930s, populists today have been urgently demanding decisive state action— sometimes liberal reforms, but often illiberal interventions—to correct liberalism’s dysfunctions. In this sense we have indeed been going “back to the future.”

Getting liberalism back on track will require fixing all four of liberalism’s basic operating systems. In the contest against illiberal forces at home and abroad, these four systems are mutually and necessarily reinforcing.
